content: Fordyce spots, also known as Fordyce granules, Fordyce disease, or Fordyce bodies, are visible sebaceous glands that are present in most individuals. These spots are typically found on the genitals and/or in the mouth. They appear as small, painless, raised spots or bumps that are pale, red, or white in color, measuring approximately 1 to 3 millimeters in diameter. Common locations include the scrotum, the shaft of the penis, the labia, the inner surface of the lips (retromolar mucosa), and the vermilion border of the lips. These spots are not associated with any disease or illness, nor are they infectious. They are considered a natural anatomical variation of the body. Treatment is not required unless the individual has cosmetic concerns. Some individuals consult dermatologists due to concerns that these spots may be sexually transmitted diseases (such as genital warts) or cancer. Sebaceous glands are normal adnexal structures of the dermis but can also be found ectopically within the mouth, where they are referred to as oral Fordyce granules or ectopic sebaceous glands. On the foreskin, they are called Tyson's glands, which should not be confused with hirsuties coronae glandis. When located on the penis, they are also referred to as penile sebaceous glands. When these glands appear as a streak along the interface between the skin of the lip and the vermilion border, the terms Fox-Fordyce disease or Fordyce's condition may be used. On the shaft of the penis, Fordyce spots become more visible when the skin is stretched and may only be noticeable during an erection. They can also appear on the scrotal skin. Oral Fordyce granules resemble rice-like granules that are white or yellow-white in color. These are painless papules, measuring about 1 to 3 millimeters in size. The most common site is along the line between the vermilion border and the oral mucosa of the upper lip or on the buccal mucosa (inside the cheeks) in the commissural region, often bilaterally. They may also occur on the mandibular retromolar pad and tonsillar areas, although any oral surface can be involved. There is no surrounding mucosal change. Some individuals may have hundreds of granules, while most have only one or two. Occasionally, several adjacent glands may coalesce into a larger cauliflower-like cluster, resembling sebaceous hyperplasia of the skin. In such cases, it may be challenging to differentiate the lesion as sebaceous hyperplasia or sebaceous adenoma. However, this distinction is often irrelevant since both conditions have the same treatment, although adenomas have a greater growth potential. It is worth noting that sebaceous carcinoma of the oral cavity has been reported, presumably arising from Fordyce granules or hyperplastic foci of sebaceous glands. In some individuals with Fordyce spots, the glands may express a thick, chalky discharge when squeezed. Sebaceous glands are typically associated with hair follicles. However, Fordyce spots are more prominent in individuals with oily skin types, certain rheumatic disorders, and hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer. In the latter condition, the most common site for Fordyce spots is the lower gingiva (gums) and vestibular mucosa. Large numbers of lobules coalescing into a distinctly elevated mass may be referred to as benign sebaceous hyperplasia. Occasionally, small keratin-filled pseudocysts may be observed and must be differentiated from epidermoid cysts or dermoid cysts with sebaceous adnexa. Pathologists must carefully distinguish these lesions from salivary neoplasms containing sebaceous cells, such as sebaceous lymphadenoma and sebaceous adenoma, as well as their malignant counterparts, sebaceous lymphadenocarcinoma and sebaceous carcinoma. Oral Fordyce granules are usually not biopsied because they are readily diagnosed clinically, but they are often seen incidentally in mucosal biopsies of the buccal, labial, and retromolar mucosa. These granules resemble normal sebaceous glands of the skin but lack hair follicles and almost always lack a ductal connection to the surface. The glands are located just beneath the overlying epithelium and often produce a local elevation of the epithelium. Individual sebaceous cells are large, with central dark nuclei and abundant foamy cytoplasm. The surrounding stroma may contain occasional chronic inflammatory cells due to trauma from adjacent teeth. Fordyce spots are completely benign and require no treatment. Their presence is often considered a normal anatomical variant rather than a true medical condition. However, for individuals with cosmetic concerns, vaporizing laser treatments such as CO2 laser or electrodessication have been used with some success to reduce their appearance. Pulsed dye lasers, commonly used to treat sebaceous gland hyperplasia, have also been employed with varying success. These treatments are expensive but may result in less scarring compared to other methods. No treatment is required for oral Fordyce granules unless cosmetic removal of labial lesions is desired. Inflamed glands can be treated topically with clindamycin. When surgically excised, they do not recur. Neoplastic transformation is extremely rare but has been reported. This anatomical variation is observed in the majority of adults. It is estimated that approximately 80% of people have oral Fordyce spots, although large numbers of granules are rarely found. They are not usually visible in children and tend to appear around age 3, becoming more prominent during puberty and increasingly noticeable in later adulthood. They are more prominent in males. Examples reported in cancer screenings represent approximately 1% of adults. Fordyce spots are named after John Addison Fordyce, an American dermatologist.
